summary: The note introduces sous-vide cooking, a technique of vacuum-sealing food and cooking it in a precisely controlled water bath, and argues it lets home cooks produce restaurant-quality entrees. It covers the history, the science, the equipment (vacuum sealer and immersion circulator), the process steps, flavor and health benefits, and diverse applications, with quotes from chefs, a scientist, and bloggers at various events.
one_line: An overview of sous-vide cooking for home dinner parties, covering its science, equipment, process, flavor and health benefits, and applications.
key_facts: Sous-vide is a French term meaning "under vacuum"; food is vacuum-sealed in a bag and cooked to a precise temperature in a water bath.

Sous-vide emerged in the mid-20th century but only gained significant traction in home kitchens in the late 2000s, having previously been reserved for high-end restaurants due to equipment cost and complexity.
Chef Julianne Vasquez hosted a sous-vide seminar in New York City on November 15, 2023, calling it "the great equalizer in the kitchen."
Dr. Emilia Morgan of the Boston Institute for Food Research said on February 3, 2024, that sous-vide gives control over exact temperature and duration, affecting texture, flavor, and moisture.
Home sous-vide requires two main pieces of equipment: a vacuum sealer and an immersion circulator, which maintains and circulates the water at the set temperature.
Modern immersion circulators, like those demonstrated at the Chicago Home Cook Expo on September 30, 2023, are sleek, user-friendly, and increasingly affordable.

The process: season and bag the ingredients, vacuum-seal, set the immersion circulator's temperature and time in a water-filled pot, place the bag in the bath, and optionally finish with a sear on a pan, grill, or torch.
Culinary blogger Sophia Martin praised the 'set and forget' appeal of sous-vide in her October 12, 2023, podcast episode "The Subtle Magic of Sous-Vide."
Chef Marcus Yee prepared sous-vide duck breast infused with orange zest and star anise at the Culinary Institute of San Francisco on December 14, 2023, saying flavors are locked in and concentrated.
Dr. Richard Kim presented a study at the Global Health Conference on January 21, 2024, showing vegetables cooked sous-vide retained nearly 90% of their vitamins, more than steaming or boiling.
Sous-vide also requires less oil or fat because the vacuum-sealed environment retains moisture.
Sous-vide applies to fruits, vegetables, desserts, and cocktails as well as meats, and suits delicate items like fish or ripe fruit.
Linda Swift's blog "Gourmet Array" shares weekly sous-vide recipes, from beef bourguignon to poached pears, including a September 20, 2023, entry on sous-vide lemon curd.
